strengths: Introduces a well-motivated formalization of payload recoverability along two complementary axes (tokens→buckets, buckets→secret), grounded in classifier-based steganalysis literature, which gives a principled way to compare steganographic schemes rather than relying on ad hoc distributional metrics.

The embedding-space hyperplane encoding/bucketing scheme is a conceptually elegant idea that ties the covert channel to the model's own learned geometry, and the paper empirically demonstrates it simultaneously improves exact-match accuracy and reduces recoverability across multiple models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B) and two datasets, which is a non-trivial joint result.

The theoretical KL-divergence and perplexity lower bounds (Theorems 7.1/7.2) provide a principled argument for why standard distributional steganalysis is fundamentally limited for fine-tuning-based attacks, adding rigor beyond purely empirical claims.

The mechanistic interpretability detection approach (linear probes on late-layer activations) is a novel and interesting defense angle, and the secret-conditioned XOR-masking control is a thoughtful ablation that convincingly decouples output-level recoverability from internal detectability, strengthening the paper's central claim that internal signatures persist even when output decoding is prevented.

Reasonably extensive experimental scope: full vs. LoRA fine-tuning, in-distribution and out-of-distribution prompt generalization, and multiple text-quality metrics (coherence, stability, perplexity, KL), with appendix details supporting reproducibility (hyperparameters, classifier configurations, probe protocols).
weaknesses: Despite the reported relative gains (+78-123%), absolute exact-match accuracies remain modest (roughly 19-43%), and results are inconsistent across settings (e.g., minimal or negative gains for Ministral-8B full fine-tuning, occasional underperformance cases), which tempers claims about the practical severity/generalizability of the improved attack.

The recoverability metric is instantiated with a specific, limited set of classifiers (XGBoost, MLP); the paper acknowledges but does not empirically test more sophisticated seed-recovery or cryptanalytic approaches an adversary might use, so the claimed reduction in recoverability could be optimistic.

The proposed mechanistic detection method assumes white-box access to hidden states, a strong assumption that the authors themselves flag as a limitation; no output-only or black-box detection baseline is evaluated, and there is no comparison against existing steganalysis detectors (e.g., classifier-based methods cited in related work) to contextualize how much of an advance the probing approach represents.

The theoretical bounds in Section 7 are derived under simplified assumptions (e.g., a specific peaked-distribution example, single hyperplane pooling) and are not directly validated against the empirical text-quality measurements in Section 6.4, which only use 1 bit/token; the connection between the theory (arbitrarily high bit-rate) and the empirical setting is left largely qualitative.

As a paper advancing an actual data-exfiltration attack method, the ethical framing is fairly brief; more detail on the responsible disclosure process or concrete mitigation guidance beyond the proposed (white-box-only) detection method would strengthen the ethics treatment given the described threat model explicitly targets institutions handling sensitive data.

strengths: Addresses a timely and interesting problem: steganographic exfiltration via fine-tuned LLMs, extending the recent TrojanStego line of work with a more rigorous formalization.

The two-axis payload recoverability metric (Rbucket, Rsecret) is a clean, classifier-based formalization that meaningfully clarifies what 'recoverable' means for covert channels, improving on prior ad hoc notions.

The theoretical bounds (Theorems 7.1 and 7.2) showing that large payloads can be hidden while KL divergence and perplexity remain within normal fine-tuning ranges are a nice, clearly argued theoretical contribution that motivates moving beyond standard steganalysis.

The XOR-masking control (Section 7.4) is a thoughtful ablation that attempts to cleanly decouple output-level decodability from internal detectability, strengthening the overall detection argument in principle.
Reasonably broad experimental scope across model sizes/types (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B; full and LoRA fine-tuning; multiple encoding/bucketing schemes and datasets).
weaknesses: Despite framing results as large relative improvements (+78%, +80%, +123%), the absolute exact-match rates remain low (19-43%), meaning the proposed 'improved' attack mostly fails in practical terms; the emphasis on relative gains somewhat overstates the practical severity of the demonstrated threat.

OOD generalization results (Table 2) are inconsistent and in many cases collapse to near 0% accuracy (e.g., all TrojanStego-trained models evaluated on Wiki prompts), undermining the claim that this is a realistic, deployable exfiltration channel; the paper itself acknowledges this is confusing ('highlights how strongly prompt structure interacts with hyperparameters') without a clear resolution.

There is a threat-model mismatch between the attack and defense sections: the attack assumes a keyless, output-only defender, while the proposed detection method (linear probes) requires white-box access to internal activations — a substantially different and stronger capability than assumed for the 'defender' in the attack formalization, limiting the coherence of the overall contribution as a unified attack/defense story.

The mechanistic detection results are not uniformly positive: bit-classification probes fail for the Embedding+Embedding scheme, and in the XOR-masking control (the most rigorous test), bit-accuracy detection succeeds in only 3 of 8 tested scenarios, weakening the central claim that fine-tuning 'leaves actionable internal signatures' robustly across settings.

The core technical novelty (random hyperplane projections in embedding space for bucketing/encoding) is a relatively incremental adaptation of ideas already used in LLM watermarking (e.g., green/red list, SemStamp), rather than a conceptually new mechanism; the contribution is largely an application/formalization exercise.

No comparison against simpler or alternative detection baselines (e.g., simple statistics on logits, embedding similarity, or non-linear probes) is provided to contextualize whether linear probing specifically is necessary or whether simpler methods would achieve comparable detection.

Some experimental configurations show unexplained anomalies (e.g., 'occasional underperformances' noted for Embedding+Embedding T and ASCII+Embedding W) that are mentioned but not analyzed, raising concerns about robustness and about whether the mechanism driving reported gains is well understood.

The practical realism of the threat model is questionable given that the secret must be included in plaintext in the prompt (inherited from TrojanStego), and the paper does not discuss how this assumption limits real-world applicability beyond acknowledging it as inherited.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code release is promised for detection but withheld for the attack side pending 'responsible disclosure,' which, combined with the complexity of the pipeline (many hyperparameters, datasets, and encoding variants), could make independent verification difficult.

strengths: Formalizes payload recoverability along two complementary, well-motivated axes (tokens→buckets and buckets→secret), providing a reusable diagnostic framework that goes beyond prior ad hoc steganalysis metrics.

The core technical idea—replacing arbitrary ASCII/parity mappings with hyperplane projections in the model's own embedding space—is a clean, principled contribution that draws a sensible analogy to watermarking literature and is shown to simultaneously reduce recoverability and improve encoding accuracy.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three model scales (8B, 8B, 70B), two fine-tuning regimes (full and LoRA), two datasets (Wiki and TrojanStego-style), and out-of-distribution prompt generalization tests, giving a fairly complete picture of the attack's behavior.

Theoretical contribution (Theorems 7.1 and 7.2) formally justifies why KL-divergence/perplexity-based steganalysis is insufficient for fine-tuning-based attacks, which is a genuinely useful argument, going beyond purely empirical claims.

The mechanistic interpretability detection approach (linear probes on late-layer activations) is a novel application to this problem, and the secret-conditioned XOR-masking control is a thoughtful experimental design that isolates internal-signature detectability from output-level recoverability.

Reasonably transparent reporting of negative/mixed results (e.g., occasional underperformance of new encodings, overfitting in full fine-tuning, inconsistent OOD generalization), which supports credibility.
weaknesses: The detection method assumes gray/white-box access to hidden states; its applicability to realistic black-box deployment scenarios (the threat model described in the introduction, where an external party only sees outputs) is left entirely as future work, which somewhat undercuts the practical significance of the defense contribution.

Absolute exact-match recovery rates for the proposed attack remain fairly low (e.g., 19-43%) even though relative improvements are large (+78-123%), making it unclear how severe the practical exfiltration threat really is compared to the baseline.

In the XOR-masking (non-decodable) control, bit-accuracy-based detection succeeds in only 3 of 8 tested scenarios, which is a meaningfully weaker result than the headline claim that detection 'persists' under non-decodable settings; the paper could more clearly caveat this inconsistency.

Security of the proposed scheme rests on the secrecy of random seeds, but the paper does not empirically evaluate robustness against seed-recovery or key-reconstruction attacks that it cites as possible (e.g., Tong et al., 2025; Tramèr et al., 2016), leaving the central 'low recoverability' claim only partially stress-tested against an adaptive adversary.

The illustrative numerical example for the KL bound (Section 7.1) relies on a specific toy distribution (peaked two-token case) rather than empirical verification against real LLM next-token distributions, so the practical tightness of the bound for actual deployments is unclear.

Results across model/encoding/dataset combinations are often inconsistent (e.g., Embedding+Embedding underperforming in some settings, full fine-tuning on Ministral behaving very differently from LoRA), and the paper does not offer a strong unifying explanation, which makes it harder to draw general design recommendations.

Presentation is dense in places (e.g., Table 2, Figure 5), with many abbreviations and configurations that require frequent cross-referencing, which could hinder readability for readers who are not already familiar with the TrojanStego baseline.

strengths: Formalizes payload recoverability along two well-motivated axes (tokens→buckets and buckets→secret) using classifier-accuracy proxies, providing a concrete, measurable notion that improves on prior informal treatments of steganographic 'stealthiness'.

The proposed embedding-geometry-based encoding/bucketing scheme is a natural and elegant idea (leveraging learned representation structure rather than arbitrary ASCII/parity rules), and it is shown to simultaneously reduce measured recoverability while improving exact-match accuracy across three different base models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B) and multiple fine-tuning regimes (LoRA/full).

Provides theoretical lower bounds (Theorems 7.1, 7.2) showing that substantial payloads can be hidden while KL divergence and perplexity remain within typical fine-tuning noise, giving principled justification for why standard steganalysis is insufficient against this class of attack.

The mechanistic-interpretability detection approach (linear probes on late-layer activations) is a genuinely novel angle for this threat model, and the secret-conditioned XOR-masking control is a clever way to decouple output-level non-decodability from internal detectability, strengthening the causal claim that fine-tuning leaves internal traces independent of output recoverability.

Broad and fairly rigorous experimental scope: OOD prompt-style generalization, text-quality metrics, downstream capability benchmarks (MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag/Winogrande), mixed-motive training to test deployability, and robustness checks (decoding temperature, tokenizer retokenization flip rates) included in appendices, which aids reproducibility and situates the attack more realistically.

Reasonably thorough and honest limitations section (threat-model assumptions, hyperplane-search scalability, output-only detection gap, symbolic-task degradation) rather than glossing over shortcomings.
weaknesses: Despite improvements, absolute exact-match rates remain modest (roughly 17-48%), and several configurations show no gain or even regressions (e.g., Embedding+Embedding on TrojanStego data, ASCII+Embedding on Wiki for Ministral Full), making the practical severity of the 'improved' attack somewhat overstated relative to the reported relative percentage gains.

The recoverability metric is defined as a max over a specific, finite set of classifier families (XGBoost, MLP); this is an empirical upper-bound proxy rather than a principled information-theoretic guarantee, and an adaptive analyst using different features (e.g., a probe trained directly to search for hyperplane structure) might recover more than reported, which is not explored.

Residual Rbucket values for the proposed embedding scheme are still well above chance (~0.6-0.7 rather than ~0.5), so the claim of an 'unrecoverable' or near-random encoding is only partially supported; the paper could more clearly delineate how much recoverability reduction is actually achieved versus merely reduced from perfect.

Capability degradation from steganographic fine-tuning is severe (up to 30+ points on standard benchmarks) and only partially mitigated by mixed-motive training (worse for full fine-tuning), raising doubts about whether the attack is practically deployable as claimed—this tension is acknowledged but not fully resolved.

Detection results are inconsistent across settings (e.g., unclear separation for Ministral-8B full fine-tuning, and bit-accuracy detection under XOR-masking succeeds in only 3 of 8 tested scenarios), which somewhat undercuts the strength of the headline detection claims.

The detection method fundamentally requires white-box access to hidden states, limiting its applicability to the more realistic black-box/API deployment scenarios that motivate the threat model in the first place; this is acknowledged only briefly as future work.

The paper covers a very large number of sub-contributions (recoverability metric, new encoding scheme, KL/PPL bounds, capability benchmarking, mixed-motive training, probe-based detection, XOR-masking control, retokenization robustness) which, combined with dense tables and abbreviations, makes the presentation difficult to follow and dilutes focus; a more streamlined narrative or additional summarization of key trends would improve clarity.

strengths: Formalizes payload recoverability via two complementary classifier-based metrics (R_bucket, R_secret), providing a more principled diagnostic than prior ad hoc steganalysis and cleanly demonstrating that TrojanStego's ASCII+parity scheme is trivially reversible.

The embedding-space hyperplane bucketing/encoding idea is a reasonably clever and well-motivated primitive that ties the covert channel to the model's own learned geometry rather than an arbitrary external code.

Theoretical KL-divergence and perplexity lower bounds for argmax promotion under bucket-constrained decoding are a nice analytical contribution that helps explain why naive distributional steganalysis is weak against this attack class.

Broad empirical coverage across three model families (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full vs LoRA fine-tuning, multiple datasets (Wiki/TrojanStego/Mixed-motive), OOD generalization, capability benchmarks, and an XOR-masking non-decodable control -- this is a substantial experimental effort.

The mechanistic-probe detection result, especially its persistence under the non-decodable XOR-masking control and under mixed-motive training, is an interesting and somewhat non-obvious finding that internal traces survive even when output-level recoverability is suppressed.

Honest and fairly detailed limitations section (threat-model assumptions, symbolic-task degradation, hyperplane-search scaling, output-only detection) and useful appendix analyses (retokenization robustness, temperature robustness).
weaknesses: Absolute exact-match accuracies remain low across the board (roughly 17-48%), and the headline framing in the abstract/conclusion in terms of large relative gains (+78%, +80%, +123%) is somewhat misleading presentation given the small absolute improvements and the fact that no single encoding scheme (A+E, E+E, E+P) is consistently best across models/datasets -- this undercuts the significance of the claimed attack improvement.

Capability degradation under the single-objective steganographic attack is severe (10-30+ percentage points on MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag/Winogrande in Table 3), and even the proposed mixed-motive mitigation leaves 20-25 pp degradation for full fine-tuning; this raises doubts about whether the attack is practically deployable, which is central to the paper's motivating threat model.

The 'low-recoverability' claim is only validated against the specific classifier families used (XGBoost/MLP) with a fixed seed set; there is no evaluation against an adaptive adversary who explicitly searches over candidate hyperplane seeds/thresholds (a natural and cheap attack given the low-dimensional embedding space), so the recoverability reduction may be weaker than presented.

The detection method (linear probes on late-layer activations) requires white-box hidden-state access, which is inconsistent with the paper's own threat model describing private/air-gapped deployment and a defender who can 'inspect and query' but is not guaranteed hidden-state access; the practical applicability of the defense contribution is therefore narrower than the framing suggests, and this is only partially acknowledged in the limitations.

The theoretical KL/perplexity bounds rely on simplified, somewhat cherry-picked numerical assumptions (e.g., a specific peaked two-token distribution with p1=0.5, p2=0.3) and are never empirically validated at the higher bits-per-token regime the theorems are meant to justify (experiments only encode 1 bit/token), leaving a gap between the theoretical motivation for the detection section and the empirical study actually performed.

Only KL divergence/perplexity are treated as representative of 'traditional steganalysis'; other established steganalysis approaches mentioned in related work (linguistic/statistical feature classifiers, semantic-similarity detectors) are not empirically compared against, so the claim that steganalysis broadly 'requires approaches beyond traditional' methods is not fully substantiated.

Heavy notational and abbreviation overload (MF/ML/LF/LL/70, A+P/A+E/E+E/E+P, W/T/M) makes the tables and results difficult to parse, and several results (e.g., Table 2 OOD generalization, Table 4 XOR detection) are reported with limited discussion of why particular configurations succeed or fail, reducing interpretability of the empirical narrative.

Many comparative claims (e.g., which encoding is 'best') are made without consistent statistical testing given the reported error bars (e.g., Table 1 entries with overlapping ±2-8 point confidence ranges), making it unclear whether some of the highlighted differences are robust.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and clearly stated formalization of 'payload recoverability' (R_bucket, R_secret) via classifier accuracy, filling a genuine gap in prior steganalysis work that conflated distributional detectability with actual decodability.

The embedding-space hyperplane-based encoding/bucketing scheme is a natural and elegant idea (reusing the model's own learned geometry rather than arbitrary rules like ASCII/parity), and the paper convincingly shows it both improves exact-match accuracy (up to +123% relative) and substantially lowers recoverability compared to TrojanStego's trivially-reversible parity scheme.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: closed-form KL-divergence and perplexity lower bounds (with full KKT-based proofs in the appendix) formally justify why standard distributional steganalysis is insufficient against fine-tuning-based attacks, which strengthens the motivation for the proposed mechanistic detection approach.

The linear-probe detection method is a nice contribution on its own, and the secret-conditioned XOR-masking control (Section 7.5) is a clever experimental design that decouples internal detectability from output-side recoverability, providing convincing evidence that mechanistic signals persist even when the payload is provably non-decodable from outputs.

Very thorough empirical study: multiple models (8B/70B, LoRA/full fine-tuning), OOD generalization tests, text-quality and capability-benchmark degradation analysis, a mixed-motive training regime to address capability loss, and appendix robustness checks (decoding temperature, tokenizer retokenization flip rates) that go beyond what is typical for a single paper.
Clear, honest limitations section addressing threat-model conditionality, symbolic-task degradation, hyperplane-search scalability, and the white/gray-box nature of the detection method.
weaknesses: Absolute exact-match rates remain fairly low even with the proposed improvements (e.g., 19-43%), which somewhat tempers the practical severity of the 'improved' attack despite the large relative percentage gains emphasized in the abstract/title claims.

The recoverability metric (max over a specific, non-exhaustive family of classifiers: XGBoost/MLP/logistic regression) is only an empirical lower bound on true recoverability, not a certified upper bound; a more sophisticated or adaptive analyst (e.g., a transformer-based decoder, or one aware of the hyperplane-projection structure) might achieve higher recoverability than reported, so claims of 'low recoverability' should be read as relative to the tested classifier families rather than as a worst-case guarantee.

The detection method's strongest results require access to internal hidden states (white/gray-box), limiting applicability to closed-source/API deployment scenarios that are arguably the most realistic threat model for the exfiltration attack itself; this asymmetry between attack (deployable in black-box settings) and defense (requires internal access) is acknowledged but not resolved.

Capability degradation from bucket-constrained generation is substantial in single-objective settings (10-30+ pp drop on standard benchmarks) and only partially recovered by mixed-motive training (worse for full fine-tuning), raising questions about whether the full attack (especially with strong steganographic signal) would actually be deployed in practice without being caught by capability regression testing.

Presentation is dense in places—Table 1 and Table 2 pack a large number of configurations/abbreviations into small tables that are difficult to parse quickly, and the relationship between the many encoding/dataset/model combinations could be summarized more clearly (e.g., with a compact takeaway figure) for readability.

The paper combines two fairly distinct contributions (a stealthier attack, and a detection method) that are only loosely coupled by narrative; while both are reasonable, a reader focused on defense might wish for more discussion of how a real defender would operationalize the probe-based detector at deployment scale (e.g., false positive rates on wholly benign fine-tuned models).
